speechtext:
I have only been in the house a short time. At least, that is what it seems to me. In that period I have seen two reforms. Last year the hours were changed and this year we are back on the same old hours. I think we should adjourn at ten o'clock at night and that a man should be able to go home and sleep a little while before twelve. The other reform we have had is that ladies were allowed to go into the gallery without their hats. We have that reform today. Perhaps we will see more of it in the spring of the year when they are getting tired of their old hats anyway. I think that the ladies should be allowed to knit in the gallery. There are clubs knitting for the Red Cross, war services and relief causes. If the ladies
Standing Orders
got tired or could hear somebody then they could knit, enjoy themselves and serve their country.
There is another reform I should like to mention. I have spoken of it before. You, Mr. Speaker, stand up reverently in the house and lead us in worship but the galleries are empty. Not even the representatives of the press are allowed to enter. The prayer you use in your service is in keeping with the teachings -of the Great Teacher who said that whosoever will may come. I hope that this reform will take place soon and that people will be allowed in the gallery to join with us in bowing their heads and worshipping the Supreme Being.
I know that a book on science ten years old is out of date with the exception of the science of government. The science of government certainly does need to be reformed, and the hon. member for Halton said that the rules of the house need to be amended and improved. If we do not improve them it is a sign that we are not doing what we should, but the word "liberal" means reform without any "pro" before it or "co" or "so" tacked on it. It means that we can grow and reform.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEBATES AND PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not be very long in presenting a few of my viewpoints about the rules of the House of Commons. Before I proceed I want to pay a tribute to the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) for his resolution which has given us an opportunity to discuss at some length a matter that has not only been before the public but before parliament for many years; namely the reform of the rules and procedures of the Canadian House of Commons. A day such as this makes every parliamentarian and every Canadian realize the logic, the artistry, if I may call it that, of the British parliamentary system on which our own parliamentary system is largely based. Early in the session there is an opportunity to discuss resolutions brought forward by private members. I do not believe there are many democracies that have perfected that system to such a degree, and I for one, although I am in favour of the drastic changes in our present procedures and rules, will go slowly as far as some of them are concerned because after all we are considering procedures which have -been tried and tested not only for years -but for centuries, but which in our times are not fulfilling their purposes.
I want to say a few words about a statement made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill). He referred to the time taken by ministers of the crown. I think it would be unfair for me to mention the time of the house that has been taken on

Standing Orders
some discussions, and rightly so, by the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Drew) for the simple reason that the leader of the official opposition, no matter what the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre may think, has more responsibility than the average member of parliament. The same principle applies just as forcibly, if not more so, to the ministers of the crown and particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) because after all they have the responsibility of bringing legislation before parliament. They have the responsibility of presenting it in a forceful and clear way and of presenting it in a manner that will be understood by every member of the House of Commons with all the necessary details. That is why I do not like that kind of reflection and comparisons are generally odious. I do not like the insinuation that ministers of the crown have been taking more time than they should have. I for one have been here for many years and I have never found a case under any conditions or circumstances where I felt that I had the responsibility on my shoulders that a minister of the cabinet has on his, and subject to criticism if their statements were not fully and clearly presented.
I also listened very attentively this afternoon to the speech of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), who was very active on the rules committee last year. In his remarks I thought he showed good judgment, as he does in all instances; but there was one thing with which I do not agree. He almost regretted that he did not read his speech this afternoon. Let me tell the hon. member that while his remarks may not read so well in Hansard, while the phraseology may not be just as chiselled as he would like, his personality with vibrancy was brought to us this afternoon; his eloquence was displayed once again. That is something you cannot put in print; yet it was felt in this parliament and in the galleries. So on that score alone I believe the house will gain a great deal if speeches are not read. The hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier) thinks the reading of speeches is a good thing for the house. My view is that this House of Commons is becoming more and more like a conference or a reading room; and that was never the intention that it should be so. I know my own constituency sent me here and after receiving their directive and after having been in contact with them for many years, and they want me to express their sentiments as I understand them, no matter how bad my delivery may be or how poor my English pronunciation.
Another practice in this house which I think is deplorable, and which has come into
[Mr. Bradette.l
being only in the last thirty years, is the quoting of citations from newspapers, editorials and periodicals. It almost seems that some hon. members are not able to put two words together unless they have a quotation to help them. This is not parliamentarianism; they are not expressing their own sentiments. I think it would help shorten the sessions if all members would try to express their own ideas, as I know they want to, and express themselves in a very practical way, which they can always easily do.
When I make that statement I have in mind one of my dear colleagues from northern Ontario, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Little), who is ill at the present time and for whom we all hope a speedy recovery. In all the years this fine man has been in the House of Commons he has not spoken more than half a dozen times, and never more than five or ten minutes at a time. But his speeches were right to the point; they were logical, and were appreciated not only by members of this house but by his own constituents, and he gave all his time and talents to his duties as an M.P. That is the kind of parliamentarianism my electors at least expect from me, and that is what is expected from all of us.
So I do not believe members should be allowed to read their speeches; and when I say that, Mr. Speaker, I mean no reflection upon you, for I believe you have done a wonderful job if any Speaker ever has. A member may have been helped in preparing his speech, but he should make' a point of giving it in his own language; he will give a better speech. I remember one occasion when two very good members had well written speeches which I do not believe they took time to analyse or scrutinize. The first thing they knew they were saying some things in this house they never intended to say and for that reason alone they were defeated at the next election. These are things which are worth considering by a member of parliament.
As far as I am concerned I hope and pray that rule will be implicitly obeyed; and that is quite possible. I do not say the Prime Minister or the members of the cabinet or the leader of the opposition or those who speak for them should not be allowed to prepare their speeches, because it would be impossible for them to improvise on the very important problems they have to discuss. As far as the average member of parliament is concerned, however, my experience is that if he is left to himself he is much more eloquent and receives much more attention from the house and also from the galleries if he does not read his speech.

As most hon. members are aware, for three years I served as Deputy Speaker of the House of Commons. That was during war, when we were dealing with the war appropriation bills, which concerned nearly all departments of government and which dealt with billions of dollars. During those years we spent three or four months on that bill alone. One of the things I cherish about those years is the wonderful co-operation I received from every section of this house. One day a member of the Progressive Conservative party thought he had been harsh with me, and before we adjourned at six o'clock he came over and said, "Joe, I am very sorry." I replied, "Don't be sorry. I know what you said came from the head, not from the heart." It was always a surprise to me that under our rules we could get through our sessions during the war years in five, six or seven months. If hon. members had not tried to play the game and to abide by the rules it would have been possible to spend the whole year here.
Of course we all realize, as the public realize, that to be elected in our own constituencies we must have something of the gift of the tongue, we must be able to express our sentiments. On every measure that comes before this house there is the natural temptation for each of us to get on our feet and speak. You can readily realize what would happen if we followed that impulse. We all understand that a certain amount of individual and collective discipline is necessary on the part of hon. members. This afternoon the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) mentioned party discipline and referred to the whips and so on. I can tell the hon. member I have been here for over a quarter of a century, and I still have to hear from the whips any directive as to how I should vote on any matter. I say that very sincerely. After all, we are free people when we come here. We are the masters of our own actions and only responsible to our electors. At the same time I am sure the hon. member and his own leader realize perfectly well that unless a certain amount of direction is given within all the parties the result will be chaos, not only within the party but in our whole parliamentary system in most of our activities. So I hope such charges will never again be levelled, because I cannot visualize a single member of this house being a servile servant either to a whip or to his own party and I never heard of a whip using undue pressure.
At the same time there is need for a certain amount of co-ordination, and I speak very feelingly on that score. At times measures
Standing Orders
brought in by our own government are not very popular in some sections of the country.
I will always remember one budget a number of years ago, when Mr. Ilsley brought the Canadian dollar to par. That was a blow to the gold mining industry of my section, as it was a blow to the constituency of the hon. member for Timiskaming. It would have been easy for me to vote against my own party on that measure, but I knew that in bringing the Canadian dollar to parity the government was doing a thing which was good for Canada as a whole; and when I received a mandate from my people it was not to represent just my own constituency but to represent the whole of Canada, because this is a central house for Canadian politics. So we went into our constituencies and told our people that though the measure was going to hurt a fine industry, at the same time it was better for Canada and the Canadian people as a whole. As a result we were never criticized on that score, as our constituents understood the situation.
I repeat, and I address myself particularly to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that there is no such thing as trying to make slaves of us as far as the party is concerned. That would not be Canadianism; that would not be any part of the Canadian system. I do not believe he ever tried it in his own party, and I think that statement applies equally to other parties in this house. We are free men representing free people in a free parliamentary institution. If parliament should decide to pass this resolution I believe it would solve most of the problems we are facing at the present time; it practically means the implementation of all the changes that we intend to make.
I repeat that if everyone wanted to speak on all subjects it would be utterly impossible for parliament to finish its work within twelve months. It is not fair for members to say that they must speak on all occasions, because if this was done the work of parliament would never be done. For instance, only last Friday that fine newspaper the Montreal Star mentioned the fact that after the minister had spoken in the debate on national defence, there were no spokesmen from the Liberal side. To some extent there was an insinuation or a criticism of this party. I cannot believe, as some members say, that the opposition members have a greater obligation than the members on this side. After all, we also have a responsibility towards our constituents and to this parliament. If we wanted to use mathematics as a basis, which cannot be applied to any parliamentary system, it would be possible for us on this side to speak as often as the members on the other side.

Standing Orders
What would be the result? The session would be prolonged almost indefinitely, but there would be no reason for criticizing those on the government side, if they decided to do so.
For five years I sat on the opposition side of the house, and to some extent they were happy years because we could express our sentiments on almost anything; we could get on our feet almost any time. However, as a man who has been loyal to his party I do not wish to make an issue of it because it is a good party with good leadership. The same thing applies just as forcibly to the other parties. The members belong to good parties with good leadership. For instance, sometimes I have had to follow the directive of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) when he has said: "Joe, spare us one of your fine speeches today because we want to get through with the measure." I complied with the request, which was a fair one. I never spoke on these matters, and I have never regretted it. It is possible to have these limitations within the other parties, and it would make for better results in our deliberations.
This afternoon the member for Peel put forward some new aspects of the subject, and I admire him for it. However, he tried to strike quite a blow at the ministers by saying that before the orders of the day are called on many occasions they make lengthy statements to the house. If I correctly understand his party's views on several occasions they have blamed the government for not giving enough information, so I do not know where the ministers should begin or stop. After all that is the proper time for a minister to give the house information to answer questions, some of them asked the previous day. So far as I am concerned personally, I feel that the member for Peel is very glad of the information given. Under our system it is possible for the government not only to give information through members of the cabinet but also through private members who may express their sentiments, and this is always conducive to good legislation.
Although I do not believe in the motto I often hear it said that the primary duty of the opposition is to oppose. In my opinion that principle is not dynamic enough nor strong enough, it is too sterile, too static. The opposition has a duty to be more than passive. Without divulging any secrets I may say that when I was deputy speaker the fine old gentleman who was on my left used to say to me on several occasions that one of the great features of the Liberal party was that anything good propounded by the Conservative party or any other
CMr. Bradette.]
party was made their own in no time. This could be one of the good features of the opposition parties too, and the mere role of opposing is not constructive enough to be helpful to that party.
Last year I was in favour of the sitting hours that we adopted, although in my own mind I was not convinced that it would be conducive to shortening the session. Unless we shorten the length of the speeches to at least thirty minutes, then I do not know where we would end. You cannot cut down the time of sitting, and at the same time maintain the length of the speeches without lengthening the session. It is humanly impossible. I say that quite sincerely. If we were not in favour of shortening the speeches we would come to the same situation we face in all sessions. Towards the end of the session, after we have had a general discussion on nearly all the measures and all the departments leaving only the statutory items, about which most of us can do nothing, we would have to stay here three or four weeks, sitting mornings, afternoons and nights, just as we have done in the past. This is a terrific ordeal for every one of us who has to stay until the end of the session. I repeat that if we want to modernize our procedure we must, to some extent, copy the British parliamentary system and adopt the suggestions in paragraphs (a) (b) (c) (d) (e) of the resolution.
We would not lose very much by adopting most of the British system. I do not mean that these changes should all be made this session. We should try to eliminate repetition. When I was the deputy speaker-I am speaking to you from my experience- the most difficult problem was to keep speakers on the subject. When we considered the estimates of the Department of National Defence, for example, we had a general discussion on. the administration item which at times lasted for days. When we were considering the different items it took me all my time to keep members of parliament on the beam, as we say. You cannot make human nature other than it is-and it is a fine thing that it is so-and that illustrates to some extent the urgency for the allocation, of time during the speech from the throne and the budget debate, as well as some important governmental measures on which a lot of leeway is given to the members of all parties to express their opinions but the number of speakers should be very limited. For instance, take the government party. On a certain measure two or three members will speak because they are familiar with the problem. The same principle should be applied in the same manner to the other parties. They all could

have two or three members who are studying the matter mentioned in a certain bill, and they would be the only ones that would speak on it. It would be quite easy to know in advance how many speakers there would be on each subject, and then you could allocate a certain time for the debate. If we adopted that method, it would be one of the finest ways of modernizing the procedure in this house.
It is true that some members of parliament believe it is necessary for them to speak, otherwise some of them will not be here after the next general election. They are afraid their opponents will say, "We have paid you $10,000 for one year and you never made one speech". So far as I am concerned, if I look after my departmental work, if I am active in my committee work, if I look after my correspondence carefully, if I receive my constituents as visitors in my home-I never keep any office hours-I need never worry about the next election, even if I did not make a speech here. After all, there are several other ways for members of parliament to utilize their knowledge, their activities. There are committees of this house in which members could spend a lot of time, and. their time would be usefully employed. I do not say this in a critical way, but I notice that some members who are great debaters on the floor of the house are often not very active committee men. In my opinion that is a sad thing because those men, with their fine analytical minds and with their knowledge of certain aspects of our Canadian life, could do a marvellous job in committees, although they would not get the same publicity there that one gets on the floor of the house. Speaking personally, I spend at least four or five hours every week in government departments working for my constituents, and that takes up quite a bit of time and activities. I do not believe members of parliament need to worry if they do not make speeches in the House of Commons because their constituents would be quite satisfied if they realized their representative was being a true servant of the people.
I thank the house for the kind attention it has given to me, and I wish to compliment again the hon. member for Halton for his fine presentation. The discussion has been good. It has been an illuminating discussion because many many angles have been brought forward, which have not been brought forward heretofore in the House of Commons and all speakers expressed themselves forcibly. All through the thread of the discussion you could readily see the demand, the inner
Standing Orders
demand, of every member of this house to see the rules of parliament revised and modernized.
Even during this debate, and in previous debates, owing to the heavy national majority that the government has, there was talk of steam rolling and so on, which statements are simply ridiculous. Well, I must make this statement. Perhaps the time is not over-ripe to amend our rules of procedure, but the time may come before very long that we may have to do it. Public opinion will request it because, although this is not a business organization or institution, we must to some extent modernize every aspect of our parliamentary system realizing the new situations and conditions that we have to face so that every member of parliament will be given an opportunity to take part in the activities and thereby conduce to shorter sessions. If we do that I believe that we shall be accomplishing great and needed work. I repeat, the time may come, even if the house is not unanimous in the reform and in the amendments to the rules of the house, when the majority in the house may have to have its voice heard on that score and have these changes passed by the majority.
Last year we put into practice some new experiments in the rules committee under your fine leadership, Mr. Speaker. We came to a unanimous decision only on the hours of sitting. When we came to the shortening of the time of the speeches we did not have a unanimous decision. We cannot have one without the other. In this matter, as in all others, it is a matter of compromise, of give and take. I make this appeal to every member of this house. Forgetting party lines, forgetting party affiliation, let us put our minds together and modernize our parliamentary rules so that those who come after us will be very thankful indeed for what we have done, which will mean not only a lot to our parliamentary system but also to the whole of the Canadian nation.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEBATES AND PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before coming to this House of Commons I had formed the opinion that the debates that took place in this house were fixed and set by a direct set of rules. Since being in the house I have not become an authority on those rules, but I did not need to be an authority to find that the state of perfection which I had thought existed in this house does not exist at the present time, and that the rules are greatly in need of amendment, and that it is time that we brought the rules more in line with the present-day needs, as set out in the resolution presented by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver).

Standing Orders
The previous speaker, the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette), has stated that eventually we shall be obliged to amend the rules of this house because of the criticism of the public. I think there has been criticism by the public for many years. In fact, I am informed that it was the late J. W. Dafoe who described a parliamentary debate as that vast repository of talk. We have had various criticisms of the way in which the business of this house has been conducted. Some lengthy sessions have become longer and longer. It is my opinion that these sessions have been extended because of the length of the speeches that have been delivered in the House of Commons.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) made the statement this afternoon, or implied, that a member was not doing his duty unless he spoke at great length in the House of Commons. To my mind that is not the sole duty of a member of the House of Commons. As has been said by the hon. member for Cochrane, there is correspondence, departmental work, and many other things in the riding that have to be taken care of. I believe that the people of our constituencies-and I have talked to many of them-expect their business to be conducted in an efficient manner and with dispatch. They wish action and a great deal less verbiage in the house. I do not know whether hon. members are aware of the fact that by June of 1952 this parliament will have been elected three years. Out of the three years or thirty-six months that we shall have been elected, we shall have spent in session in Ottawa twenty-five months. Out of the thirty-six months we have had the opportunity to be at home for only eleven months.
It seems to me that the business of a member of parliament is not confined solely to debates in the House of Commons. I think a member has an obligation to get out about his riding and find out what is going on in the particular constituency that he represents. The way that we are going on in this house, we are apt to be living in an ivory tower in Ottawa out of touch with the common people who elect us and send us here to do their business. It is about time we had the opportunity to return to our home constituencies for a portion of each year, when we would have an opportunity to go out on the highways and by-ways of our constituencies and talk to the people and get an idea of what they know and what they feel about the issues that are being discussed here in the House of Commons.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEBATES AND PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I agree that the business of government has become more complicated in

the last twenty years, but it is not necessary to prolong debate in order that we may have a reasonably lengthy session. People in Canada are concerned because we cannot finish the business of the country in a five-month session and we are obliged to have two sessions each year. I wish to quote an excerpt from a recent editorial in the Ottawa Journal, which reads as follows:
Every member of parliament knows well that there is atrocious waste of time in parliament, debates which sensibly could be confined to a day are dragged on through weeks in complete futility.
Of course there is such a thing as freedom of speech. No one in this house denies the right of freedom of speech to those members who are elected to do the country's business; but as I have seen parliament in action, I am convinced that there is a repeated and persistent abuse of that privilege. Freedom unbridled may become licence. That is why I say I commend the hon. member for Halton for the resolution which he has placed before us tonight. I think there is a great deal of merit in that part of his resolution which limits the time of speeches in the debate on the speech from the throne, in the budget debate and in any other particular debate.
No hon. member need feel that he will not have an opportunity of expressing himself in this house. I have yet to see the time when any hon. member has been refused the right to speak during any of the debates, and I believe that would continue if a limited time were placed on each debate. Then, I think the time of speaking could be reduced from forty minutes to twenty minutes. When I was a law student some years ago, I recall very well a lecture by a former member of this House of Commons, and an eminent counsel, Mr. Arthur G. Slaght, Q.C. Mr. Slaght on that occasion told members of the class that it was impossible for the average speaker to be able to hold the attention of any group, particularly a jury, for more than half an hour. I am sure there are few members in this House of Commons who can hold the interest of the House of Commons for longer than twenty minutes, and do it successfully. Therefore I congratulate the hon. member for Halton. I hope that this resolution will come to a vote, and that it will receive the support of the majority of the members of the House of Commons.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEBATES AND PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been said that soul-searching and selfconfession have certain advantages. Indeed I remember an occasion-I think it was just at the spring session of last year-when somebody who perhaps was not overcharitable said that the Senate had never discussed anything so intelligently as when

it discussed the necessity of reforming its own rules. Applying the same feeling, I suppose one might say that the House of Commons is probably never more profitably engaged and never appears in a better light than when it is confessing its own faults, admitting its shortcomings and trying to find ways and means of devising improvements in its procedure.
That is what we have been doing a good deal of today. From what we have heard, it seems that many members feel that the house wastes too much time. There has been a process of self-accusation. If that selfaccusation results in true penitence and reform, I suppose that some good-perhaps more than appears on the surface-will have been accomplished. This thought reminded me that there is an apt verse in the bible- and I found it in chapter 15 of St. Luke- which I have just obtained from the table. I may say that I found it with the help of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who is an authority on many subjects.

speechtext: I think you will perhaps see, Mr. Speaker, that considerable good has already come from this debate, in signs of repentance on the part of hon. members. We in the opposition here have heard accusations oft repeated-and with, I think, a good deal of sincerity-that we take too much of the time of the house that is, that numbers of members of the opposition, out of all proportion to the actual size of the opposition parties, monopolize the discussion in the house at the expense of the unfortunate but numerically larger government party. I am sure that you will have observed, .Mr. Speaker, that we have already taken those admonitions to heart and that so far there have spoken in this debate seven members of the government party as against only four from the opposition benches.

speechtext:
In the course of this debate we have already heard a great deal about the question of filibuster. "Filibuster", of course, is a word which is applied by those -who wish to put through a measure and who
Standing Orders
find themselves opposed. It depends entirely on the point of view with which you approach the measure, as to whether you call the speeches made for or against the measure a filibuster or constructive criticism. Sometimes I think that we should be serious about these things, and that we should ask ourselves the question whether, in the long run, we shall do ourselves or anybody else any real good by debating so seriously the question of improving our methods here and increasing the efficiency of the House of Commons.
I am not always certain that it is a good thing to be purely efficient. I am not certain that we get only advantage from subjecting ourselves to the suggestions of efficiency experts. I was impressed by something which was said by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) in the course of his speech this afternoon

when he spoke about the problems which confront a member of parliament and the serious tasks which he has to undertake. One thing has impressed me in the course of my comparatively few years as a member of the house, and it is this. I do not think that there is anything that the members of parliament could do by way of improving the procedure here which would really meet with the approval of the people of Canada. I think that they to some extent rather like to have the House of Commons and the members of parliament whom they can always make the butt of a useful joke. That is something that is useful to a man looking around for some story to tell in a meeting.
A member sometimes gets the feeling that nothing he can do is right. If he talks in the House of Commons, he is accused of wasting time. If he remains silent in the House of Commons, he is accused of lack of interest and letting important legislation go through that is full of flaws and defects which he should have pointed out and brought to the attention of the government. If the session is long and a member stays here during the whole session, he is blamed for not coming home and meeting his constituents and for getting out of touch with the people at home. On the other hand, if he skips part of the session and goes home and is seen around his constituency, he is wrong again and is accused of being overpaid, never seeming to do any work at Ottawa. I did not know that members of parliament can ever really become perfect.

speechtext:
I am glad to know that there is one perfect member in the house. It increases one's faith in human nature and in our parliamentary institutions. It seems to me that the important thing to do in this parliament, as in any other human institution, is to make the best of the resources which are at our disposal. The resources which are at our disposal here are the human resources made up of the sum of the members of parliament who are here trying to do the best they can for their country and their constituents.
While it is true that we must occasionally give serious attention to the methods and procedures under which we work, I feel very strongly that it would be most unwise for us to take a resolution of this sort which is written down on the order paper containing suggestions which have been worked out conscientiously and simply to say that those are the changes we are going to make regardless of the opinions or feelings of those who

have some doubt as to the extent to which it will curtail the right of debate.
I do not want to repeat what has been said many times this afternoon, but I think it is important to remember that parliament is a forum for discussion. That is what the word means. I do not want to be disagreeable or critical, but I certainly must take issue with those who say that the sole function of parliament is to pass legislation. I submit most earnestly that one of the important functions of parliament is to examine legislation before it is passed. In my view that is the reason why our rules have been worked out even to the point of being in the view of some hon. members cumbersome, defective and inefficient so that it is hard to get legislation through quickly.
I should like to make one or two perhaps more serious remarks. I do agree that there is a necessity for an overhaul, perhaps improvement and some streamlining of our procedures. I sometimes think of the rules of parliament as they are in existence today as being something like the one-hoss shay about which Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote, the one that was built in such a logical way that it run one hundred years to a day and then all of a sudden, as the poem goes on, ah, but stay, I will tell you what happened without delay.
It would take me a long time to tell you what has happened to the rules of parliament, but I do believe that they are in danger of suffering from what happened to the one-hoss shay. If we do not patch them up, if we do not revise them, if we do not streamline them, if we do not try to bring them more into conformity with fundamental things, one day they may collapse about our ears in a manner similar to the one-hoss shay. The time may come when resentment builds up to such a point that we may perhaps be irritated, if you like, or consider ourselves forced into doing something rash and reckless and extreme with the rules which would result in an improper limitation of debate.
I think it is useful for us to look at our rules and I think we should approach them with the recollection that these rules were devised to deal with a country of some three million people in 1867, not quite one hundred years ago but getting on toward it, and that they have not been modified substantially or brought up to date since that time. They were sufficient for a parliament with the volume of business that existed in 1867, but they are hardly adequate to deal with the volume of business that a nation of fourteen million people has today, with all the many problems and difficulties that confront such a nation.
Standing Orders
I think we should take a good look at the House of Commons in London which has always struck me as having more elastic rules which seem to make it easier to conform to the increased pressure of business than do our rules. But I do not think we can do what the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) has suggested, and take any single set of rules or procedures for limiting debate which might be applicable to the House of Commons in London and apply them in the form of a strait-jacket, as it were, to our procedures here without undertaking certain other fundamental revisions of the rules and procedures of this house which would make them a more suitable framework around which to apply the restrictions to which the hon. member has referred.
I am not going to speak at length for the very good reason that I am not an expert on the rules either of this house or of the House of Commons in London. However, there is one thing which does strike me as the central point around which the rules of the parliament in London are made so flexible and which enables that House of Commons to curtail debate without there being any suggestion of unfairness or of the majority party forcing its will upon the minority. In my view the whole feature revolves around the position, the dignity and authority of the Speaker in the House of Commons at London.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you will believe me when I say that I speak in no sense of criticism in referring to the position of the Speaker here as not being the same as the position enjoyed by the Speaker of the House of Commons in England. If that is so it is for no other reason than that it has been our custom to change our Speakers with every parliament. As is well known, in England the Speaker is not changed with every parliament. Although it is not any part of the written law, the custom there has resulted-I may be putting it rather carelessly-in the Speaker's having a more independent position than he has here.
When the Spearker there rigidly applies some rule, enforces limitation of debate or disciplines a member, there is never any feeling that it is done for reasons of partiality. The Speaker there is absolutely impartial, and that is recognized. It seems to me that until that same fundamental principle is accepted here and we can have the same curtailment of debate as is possible over there, which would be accepted without any suggestion inside or outside the house that there was unfairness or partiality, it will be extremely difficult for us to adopt these restrictions which the hon. member for Halton has set forth in the resolution.

Standing Orders
Perhaps I can say in a few words what I perhaps have not succeeded in saying very clearly. It would not toe logical to adopt only some of the methods by which debate is curtailed in the parliament in London without adopting the other features without which the discipline necessary to insist upon that curtailment and enforce it would be non-existent or which would result in extreme resentment by members if discipline were enforced. It seems to me that it would enhance the dignity of parliament and make it more likely to have voluntary acceptance of rigid enforcement of discipline on the part of the Speaker if the Speaker's appointment in this House of Commons were permanent, as in the British House of Commons.
We have to meet certain other difficulties in Canada that do not confront the parliament in London. There is the tradition, which I think is a very proper one, that the Speaker in Canada should be on one occasion of English-speaking origin and on another occasion of French-speaking origin. But I think that could be perfectly well maintained without the frequent rotation of Speakers that we have in Canada. Whenever a Speaker chose to resign or retire and a new Speaker was appointed the same principle could be followed, but I regard it as unnecessary to change Speakers with every parliament. I believe it would raise the tone of our debate and make it possible for the Speaker to discipline us, which we all need on occasion, much more readily if the same system were followed here as is followed over there.
I do wish to say, however, that we should bear in mind always that distant fields look green, and that although there are some ways in which the procedure at Westminster perhaps is preferable to our own, nevertheless they have their trials and difficulties too. They have the same complaints about tedious debates and about too much time being given to one subject in comparison with another. That reminds me that I want to correct the record in one respect. Several references have been made to the debate on the resale price maintenance legislation at the last session. I had not realized that the views expressed by opposition members on that occasion had made such a deep impression on hon. members on the government side. We heard them this afternoon speaking of an endless and protracted debate. Indeed the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Boisvert) in referring to that debate said that they had listened to speeches for three weeks. That was not good enough for him and he increased his figure to two months. If hon. members will check the record I believe they will find the subject was discussed for four

and a half days before the Christmas break and for two days after the Christmas break. Of the four and a half days preceding Christmas one day was entirely devoted to a discussion of procedure. On that occasion the procedural discussion was not initiated by a minister of the crown but by a private member, our good friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
Therefore on a subject of tremendous importance, a step which was to bring about a change in a long established system affecting all retail business in Canada, after a debate of only three and a half days hon. members opposite were found to say that this thing was being unnecessarily and needlessly protracted, and indeed we even heard suggestions that it was time to apply closure. I suggest that we maintain a sense of proportion in all these things and that hon. members opposite as well as members on this side remember that whether or not a debate is a filibuster depends entirely upon the point of view of the person who is using that word.

Coming back to the remark with which I was about to close before I was sidetracked momentarily, I think it is important to remember that although there are certain desirable features of the procedure of the House of Commons in London they obviously have their troubles. They apparently not only have their long week-enders, their t.n.t. boys, Thursday to Tuesday, but they also have their fair share of what an hon. member sitting near me the other day called "leopards behind the curtain". According to a report about parliament appearing in Punch for March 19, it appears that in the House of Commons in London on Monday, March 10, there was one of those occasions when most of the members were engaged in meetings outside behind the curtains and in private rooms around the parliament buildings. The article in Punch has this to say:
The subject under debate on the floor was the army estimates, which were destined to keep the house until nearly three the following morning. But the greater interest lay in countless other gatherings in the palace of Westminster, at which plans for (a) the downing of the Bevanites; (b) the triumph of the Bevanites, and (c) compromise, were eagerly debated.
After listening to some of the points made by the comparatively few speakers who remained in the house and took part in the discussion, a striking similarity to what was said the other day by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) with respect to the defence debate, the article goes on to say:
It took still longer for the house to dispose of the estimates, not so much because there was anything to talk about as because it is the tradition to take a long time over the estimates. But most of the opposition side stayed at their private meetings, "out of doors," as Mr. Churchill always puts it.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEBATES AND PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
There has been again today, as there has been on very many other occasions
Standing Orders
during the last ten years since I have been here, a debate upon the desirability of making some improvements in the rules governing our sittings. There have been a number of suggestions but it has been quite as apparent today, as it was on other occasions, that it is very difficult to get anything like 250, 255 or 262 well disposed gentlemen to agree upon changes in the practices that have grown up that would constitute real improvements.
However, I have had a check made of the Journals, and since 1926 there have been more than a dozen occasions when the desirability if not the necessity of improvements has been discussed; and as the hon. gentleman who just spoke said, the rules are very much the same as when they were designed to take care of a parliament representing three million people, with affairs very much less difficult and complex than those that have to be dealt with at the present time. During the last two sessions we had experiments with changes with which some were quite well pleased and others not so well pleased. On December 13 of last year a report was submitted to this house by a select committee that had been set up to consider with Mr. Speaker the recommendations that might be made. There did not happen to be any time to give consideration to that report, because it would have been the practice to refer it to the committee of the whole. I sat through more than one day of discussion of the rules in committee of the whole which produced nothing but the interesting speeches to which we listened; and there seemed no time last session to do that. But in the report submitted at that time there are suggestions and recommendations which certainly appear to a great many to have substantial merit. No doubt suggestions have been made here today that would appear to a good many to have substantial merit.
Certainly there will not be another opportunity before Easter to get back to this question. In order that the discussion today may not be lost or wasted, like some of the former discussions in this house, might it not be advisable to reconstitute the committee to which I have just referred to consider with Mr. Speaker all these suggestions that have been made? If I had the unanimous consent of the house I would move the following motion-and I trust the mover of this resolution will not be offended at this course of action-instead of trying to reach a decision here as to whether or not the precise form of this resolution could or should be adopted:
That a select committee composed of members to be named later be appointed to consider with Mr. Speaker this resolution (Mr. Cleaver's motion)

Standing Orders
and the debate thereon, together with the proposals and suggestions contained in the report of the select committee on the procedure of this house presented on December 13, 1951, with power to send for persons and papers and to report from time to time its findings and recommendations to the house, and that the said resolution be now referred to the select committee thus appointed.
That select committee might again recommend some further trials, if not definite changes in the rules. A number of hon. members on both sides of the house, or if not both sides at least belonging to the parties habitually seated on the respective sides of the house, would favour, as I gathered from the applause that marked some of the statements made in the course of the debate, the adoption of the hours we were using toward the end of last session. Even if we got no further than that and did not have the qualification the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) felt was necessary, that is to say a concurrent decision to restrict speeches to thirty minutes, I am sure a large number of members-I do not know whether it would be anything like unanimous-would prefer the hours we were using and would feel that by self-discipline we might make up the time those hours would take from the regular week. I think if we did reappoint this select committee it could make another try, and I would hope something constructive would come from it.
There is much to be said for the point of view expressed by the hon. member who last spoke as to the impossibility of fitting into our system parts taken out of the rules of practice of the parliament at Westminster. They have been the result of a gradual growth accompanied by qualifications which we might not have as an accompaniment if we embodied them in our own standing orders and proceedings. It has been suggested for perhaps two or three sessions that we could fix separate debates. Well, this year we had a separate debate on external affairs. We have one on defence that has not yet been completed but which I hope may be completed tomorrow. It may be we will find that is something that makes for an improvement in the order of debate.
I think much is to be said for the suggestion by the hon. member that the authority of the Speaker over the House of Commons at Westminster is very great, and helps to maintain an orderly conduct of the discussions without any feeling of resentment. Well, I do not wish to be unduly complimentary, sir, but it is my impression that during the sessions you have occupied that position the dignity with which the affairs of the house have been conducted and the impartiality you have displayed have been such as to give

confidence to everyone that rules with some elasticity which you might be allowed to apply would be applied in a dignified and impartial way, and that this would also help not to throttle freedom of speech but to eliminate unnecessary repetition without there being any feeling of resentment.
I would be very reluctant to ask the house to vote by a majority something that any large section of the house felt was unfair. I do not think it would be practicable to get the work of the house done if there was a lasting feeling of unfairness in the minds of any substantial group in the house. I think that would defeat our purpose. While such modifications as we do get may not be acceptable to everyone, they should be such that no substantial group would feel that the majority was abusing its power. I think the only way to achieve that kind of result is to have these matters further considered by a committee the members of which will be suggested by the various groups. They may not be able to make many unanimous recommendations, but I would hope they would be able to have unanimous recommendations on rather more than has been found possible so far; and that in any event there would be a spirit of generosity on both sides that might allow us, for the remainder of the session after Easter, to have the hours that we had during the last session, and that the establishment of those hours would create a desire to have them operate in such a way as to not prolong the session unduly. If I have the unanimous consent of the house, I would submit this motion to re-establish this select committee, the names to be specified at a later date, and have the select committee consider this resolution, all the suggestions that have been made in the course of the debate as well as all the suggestions that the committee dealt with in the report that was tabled on December 13 last.

As to the scope, the motion provides for referring not only the resolution but the debate of today, and I think the debate has covered pretty generally everything that would be apt to be required to be considered. My intention was not to limit consideration of the committee in any way whatever, and if the committee found that the debate of today and the suggestions that are in the report of December 13, 1951, did not extend to everything that they should consider, it would be very easy for them to make a report and ask for further powers. I am sure the house would be only too glad to grant those further powers.
I trust that this committee would be a committee of the same members as at the last session, and probably the names would be readily available. They could be secured not later than Wednesday, and the committee might even have a meeting before the Easter recess; then a report would be available for consideration as soon as we got back. I am afraid that some of those who have had objections to changing the hours would feel it was not quite fair to have done it without notice, by unanimous consent of a house which was not even half filled. I hope the hon. member will feel that that is perhaps true, and my reason for taking that attitude is not that I do not want it done, but that I think it might be done in a more acceptable way if it came as a report from His Honour the Speaker and his committee.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEBATES AND PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am somewhat concerned about the actual form of this motion. I am merely anxious to put through a motion that is effective. As the motion which is before me reads, it would appear to be a separate
Standing Orders
motion, standing by itself. I am wondering how it is related to the motion of the member for Halton now before the house, to which this motion refers. May I point out that it is not drafted as an amendment to the motion by the member for Halton.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEBATES AND PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is why I asked for unanimous consent to present it. We have followed the procedure of 1930. There had been a motion of this kind before the house, and then it was moved that the original motion and amendment be referred to a committee appointed to deal with all matters connected with pensions for returned soldiers, and that the committee have power to consider the advisability of doing such and so. I thought that this would permit the resolution, the debate on the resolution, and the other matters that are not before us this session but that are expressed in the report that was tabled at the end of last session, to be referred to this committee and get the consideration of the committee. Then, they would come back to the house in the form of a report from the committee.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEBATES AND PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: It seems to me that to regularize the procedure it would be necessary for the member for Halton to withdraw his motion, then have a vote on this motion separately. As I understand, the Prime Minister is suggesting that the subject matter of the hon. member's resolution should be referred, along with the committee report that was made to the house and any suggestions that have been advanced in today's debate, to this special committee. If any other members have valuable suggestions to offer the committee, or the committee itself has some valuable suggestions, I understand they might be considered. It seems to me there is no limit to this. To get the procedure in proper order, I think the hon. member for Halton should withdraw his motion, that is without prejudice to the resolution or the subject matter of it, then the Prime Minister's motion might be carried. The whips might be asked to name a committee tomorrow morning, and possibly they could have a meeting right away.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEBATES AND PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: In 1930 it was not considered necessary for the motion which was then before the house to be withdrawn. It was a motion to have the board of pension commissioners consider pensions, and the motion was not withdrawn. It was a motion that all the words after "that" be struck out-

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEBATES AND PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: It was an amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEBATES AND PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No, it was moved that the motion and the debate on it be referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs. The hon. member for Halton told me he had

Standing Orders
no objection to withdrawing his motion, but I told him I did not think it was necessary. I thought it might be referred to the committee and that, being referred to the committee, it would disappear from the order paper. I would not wish to be discourteous to the member for Halton, so I asked him and he told me he had no objection if that were required, in order that the matter might go before the committee.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEBATES AND PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is only a question of draftsmanship, but the Prime Minister has just pointed out that the motion to which he referred, and which he is using as a precedent, actually called for the striking out of certain words of the earlier motion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEBATES AND PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, there had been a motion and an amendment, and instead of deciding either the motion or the amendment the Prime Minister moved that the motion and the amendment be referred to the committee, and it was on that precedent that this procedure was drafted. I do not think there is any point in taking much time over these procedural things. I think we are all agreed that the subject matter should be considered by this select committee under the chairmanship of the Speaker. The hon. member for Halton is, I understand, prepared to withdraw his motion. If any hon. member feels that is more desirable-I do not think it is necessary-it could be done so that we will not be embarrassed by any dispute on procedure.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEBATES AND PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I point out that it is just because these things do become precedents, as the Prime Minister himself mentioned in relation to something that happened in 1930, that I am suggesting a change in a few words that I believe would bring this in order, if the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) is withdrawing it. I suggest that it read:
That a select committee composed of members to be named- later be appointed to consider with Mr. Speaker the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Halton and the debate thereon . . .
But then that would specifically refer to the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Halton which is now being withdrawn. I am only concerned about the fact that this will stand without any subsequent argument.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEBATES AND PROCEDURE IN COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am not quite clear as to what the hon. member means. Does he suggest that with his change, the motion should be withdrawn?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we will resume the debate on the motion to go into supply and discuss national defence. We hope sincerely to conclude this debate and call an item in the following departments: trade and commerce, resources and development, national health and welfare, and labour. Then we will consider the resolution to approve a treaty of peace with Japan.
It is understood that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will make his budget speech at eight o'clock. I suppose the opposition financial critic will adjourn the debate and the house will revert to its ordinary business.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, while it may be that the government will not be willing to consider it, I do suggest the advisability of proceeding with the motion to set up a redistribution committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I myself am becoming a little muddled. I thought we had an understanding that we would have two debates; one on external affairs and one on national defence. Discussing it with my -colleagues today, I insisted that we continue this debate on defence.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Let me make this quite clear. I am not suggesting that there be an interruption of the debate on national defence. But, following the hope expressed by the minister that that debate would terminate, I was merely suggesting that when that debate terminated there might be an opportunity to proceed with the resolution dealing with redistribution.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
With respect to that, Mr. Speaker, I think I should volunteer this word of explanation. I may have to withdraw the resolution, the notice of which I have on the order paper, and substitute another, because I am told that under the rules there cannot be any amendment moved that would expand the powers of a select committee. Though I do not want to sponsor anything that I would have to oppose, I want to make it as broad as possible, so that the house can cut it down if it chooses to do so, but so that there will be no procedural obstacle in the house expressing the whole of its views. I thought I had just that in the form of the resolution that is on the order paper, but I am told I have not; that there would toe other points of view that it should be possible to discuss, but that could not be raised by amendments that would be in order to the notice as I have framed it, and I have been asked to frame it in proper terms so that the other matters could by amendments to mine be properly discussed and not be ruled out of order. This is also a matter which
Business of the House
has difficulties on its merits, and I should like to avoid having procedural difficulties in the matter submitted. I feel that I am not doing this as the Prime Minister; I am doing it as the leader of the majority party, whose duty it is to provide an opportunity for a full discussion of the subject.
Another draft has been prepared, which I have submitted to the critics to see if that would allow the discussion of everything that it might be desirable to add, and I may have to ask tomorrow for permission to withdraw this notice and substitute another. I hope it may be possible to do that, and to have it ready for Wednesday, if I can get the dispensation of the forty-eight hours' notice for the new form.
I am told that my form would take care of one set of difficulties, but would raise another set of difficulties that could not be overcome by any amendment that would be in order, and that in order to make it possible to have the other set of difficulties taken care of I shall have to broaden the terms of my proposal, or the Speaker would find himself obliged to rule out of order certain amendments that it may be desired to suggest.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I agree with the Prime Minister that it is most desirable that in a matter as important as this there be no question of the adequacy of the resolution. When I made the suggestion it was with the idea that possibly the members of that committee might, if possible, meet and have certain information placed in their possession before the Easter holiday, tout I agree that it is more important that the resolution adequately cover all contingencies.
It being ten minutes after eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, April 8, 1952
